newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle set for Tuesday launch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle set for Tuesday launch.

text.p: Technicians began fuelling space shuttle Columbia on Tuesday for its planned blastoff later in the day on a 16-day science mission, NASA officials said.
Loading of a half million gallons of super-chilled liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen rocket fuel aboard Columbia's giant rust-coloured fuel tank began at dawn.

The three-hour operation was held up briefly when a leak of explosive hydrogen was detected in the shuttle's engine compartment, said NASA spokesman Bruce Buckingham. Engineers quickly solved the problem and fuelling resumed shortly after.
"We're moving right along," said Buckingham. "There's no impact to launch."
The $2 billion spaceship was due to roar away from its Florida launch pad at 2:53 p.m. EST (1953 GMT), after an 11-day delay caused by booster rocket problems and gusty winds.
U.S. Air Force meteorologists were predicting an 80 percent chance of fair weather for liftoff.

Columbia's crew of five astronauts includes Story Musgrave, who at 61 years old will become the oldest spaceflier ever. This will be his sixth trip in orbit, equalling the record currently held by veteran astronaut and moonwalker John Young.

Seven hours after blastoff, Columbia's crew will release the first of two satellites, a U.S.-German space telescope. The orbiting observatory will fly free for nearly two weeks, before the shuttle returns to pick it up.

A second satellite will be dropped off to test an innovative process for manufacturing ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry. It will orbit close to the shuttle for three days and will also be retrieved.
Astronauts Tom Jones and Tammy Jernigan will make two spacewalks to practice construction of NASA's planned international space station.
Columbia, NASA's oldest shuttle, is due to return to earth at the Kennedy Space Centre on Dec. 5.
